newsitem.title: USA: Croat minister wants U.S.-led force to stay in Bosnia.
newsitem.headline: Croat minister wants U.S.-led force to stay in Bosnia.

text.p: Croatia wants the U.S.-led peacekeeping force to remain in Bosnia through 1997, Defence Minister Gojko Susak said on Wednesday.

"IFOR should stay for another year," Susak told reporters at the Croatian embassy during a visit to meet U.S. officials and to sign a deal to buy six helicopters, the first major purchase by Croatia of American defence equipment.

IFOR, the acronym for the 60,000-member Implementation Force, is scheduled to leave Bosnia at the end of the year. The issue of having American troops in Bosnia beyond then is politically sensitive. Republicans have accused President Clinton of deceiving the public about a longer commitment.
But Susak said that 25,000 to 30,000 allied troops should remain in Bosnia for another year because "they are sending a message (to Bosnia's Serbs) that the international community is serious."
U.S. forces comprise about half the troops in Bosnia.
U.S. Defence Secretary William Perry, who will meet Susak on Thursday, issued a statement on Saturday saying that no decision had been made on keeping U.S. troops in Bosnia.

Perry called a report in the New York Times misleading. It quoted administration officials, NATO leaders and European diplomats as saying "active planning" was under way for a force of 15,000 to 30,000 troops that would remain in Bosnia at least through 1997.

Perry said NATO military advisers were considering four options and no decision had been made: complete withdrawal of the current NATO force, a "deterrence force" to prevent outbreak of fighting, a "sustaining force" to provide security in Bosnia and a continuation of the current mission.

"These options are still being analysed by NATO military authorities," Perry said. He added the analysis would not be available for some days and he had made no recommendation to President Bill Clinton.

Susak said Croatia remains concerned about Iranian influence on Bosnia's mainly Moslem Army. "Our concern is that there are still some of them present even though the (Sarajevo) government says it is not the case. Their mission there is for different purposes."
Susak said he is signing a $15 million agreement to buy six Bell helicopters for military training and the deal includes American instructors.

He also said Croatia, which until now has relied exclusively on Eastern bloc military equipment, is buying 10 fighter planes from the Swiss firm Pilatus, but would like to buy American planes in the future.
